39.2: For it is necessary that it should convert all things to itself, and fill all things, and that it should be in no respect deficient, and should not diminish its exuberance.
39.3: Let no one therefore conceive the desirable to be such as that which is frequently extended in sensibles as the object of appetite.
39.5: Nor let him suppose it to be such as is indeed able to energize upon and excite to itself the natures which are able to participate it, but which at the same time may be apprehended by intelligence, and is educed by us according to a projecting energy, and an adhesion of the dianoetic power.
39.6: For it is ineffable, and prior to all knowledge extends to all beings.
39.7: For all things desire *the good*, and are converted to it.
39.8: But if it be requisite summarily to unfold the characteristic peculiarity of the desirable, as the supplier of light proceeds by his rays into secondary natures, converts the eye to himself, causes it to be solar-form, and to resemble himself, and through a different similitude conjoins it with his own fulgid splendour, thus also I think the desirable of the Gods allures and draws upward all things to the Gods in an ineffable manner by its own proper illuminations, being every where present to all things, and not deserting any order whatever of beings.
39.9: Since even matter itself is said to be extended to this desirable, and through this desire is filled with as many goods as it is able to participate.
39.10: It is therefore the centre of all beings, and all beings, and all the Gods have their essences, powers and energies about this.
39.11: And the extension and desire of things towards this is inextinguishable.
39.12: For all beings aspire after this desirable which is unknown and incomprehensible.
39.13: Not being able therefore either to know or receive that which they desire, they dance round it, and are parturient and as it were prophetic with respect to it.
39.14: But they have an unceasing and never-ending desire of its unknown and ineffable nature, at the same time that they are unable to embrace and embosom it.
39.15: For being at once exempt from all things, it is similarly present to and moves all things about itself, and is at the same time by all of them incomprehensible.
39.16: By this motion also and this desire it preserves all things.
39.17: But by its unknown transcendency through which it surpasses the whole of things, it preserves its proper union unmingled with secondary natures.
39.18: Such therefore is the desirable. — But the sufficient is full of boniform power, proceeds to all things, and extends to all beings the gifts of the Gods.
39.19: For we conceive such a sufficiency as this to be a power pervading and protending to the last of things, extending the unenvying and exuberant will of the Gods, and not abiding in itself, but unically comprehending the super-plenitude, the never-failing, the infinite, and that which is generative of good in the divine hyparxis.
39.20: For the desirable being firmly established, and surpassing the whole of things, and arranging all beings about itself, the sufficient begins the progression and multiplication of all good, calls forth that which is primary in the uniform hyparxis of the desirable, by its own prolific exuberance, and by the beneficent replenishings which pervade to all things, and copiously produces and imparts it to every being.
39.21: It is owing to the sufficient therefore, that the stability of divine natures, and that which proceeds from its proper causes is full of goodness, and that, in short, all beings are benefited, abiding in, proceeding from, and being united to their principles, and essentially separated from them.
39.22: Through this power therefore, the intellectual genera give subsistence to natures similar to themselves, souls desire to generate, and imitate the beings prior to souls, natures deliver their productive principles into another place, and all things possess, in short, the love of generation.
39.23: For the sufficiency of the goodness of the Gods, proceeding from this goodness, is disseminated in all beings, and moves all things to the unenvying communication of good; intellect indeed to the communication of intellectual, but soul of psychical, and nature of natural good.
39.24: All things therefore abide through the desirable of goodness, and generate and proceed into second and third generations through the sufficient.
39.25: But the third thing, the perfect, is convertive of the whole of things, and circularly collects them to their causes; and this is accomplished by divine, intellectual, psychical and physical perfection.
39.26: For all things participate of conversion, since the infinity of progression is through this again recalled to its principles; and the perfect is mingled from the desirable and sufficient.
39.27: For every thing of this kind is the object of desire, and is generative of things similar to itself.
39.28: Or in the works of nature also, are not perfect things every where lovely and prolific through the acme of their beauty?
39.29: The desirable therefore establishes all things, and comprehends them in itself.
39.30: The sufficient excites them into progressions and generations.
39.31: And the perfect consummately leads progressions to conversions and convolutions.
39.32: But through these three causes, the goodness of the Gods fixing the unical power and authority of its proper hypostasis in this triad, is the primary and most principal fountain and vestal seat of things which have any kind of subsistence whatever.

40.1: In the next place let us consider the beautiful, what it is, and how it primarily subsists in the Gods.
40.2: It is said therefore to be boniform beauty, and intelligible beauty, to be more ancient than intellectual beauty, and to be beauty itself, and the cause of beauty to all beings; and all such like epithets.
40.4: But it is separate not only from the beauty which is apparent in corporeal masses, from the symmetry which is in these from psychical elegance, and intellectual splendour, but also from the second and third progressions in the Gods; and subsisting in the intelligible place of survey, it proceeds from this to all the genera of the Gods, and illuminates their superessential unities, and all the essences suspended from these unities, as far as to the apparent vehicles of the Gods.
40.5: As therefore through the first goodness all the Gods are boniform, and through intelligible wisdom they have a knowledge ineffable, and established above intellect, thus also, I think, through the summit of beauty, every thing divine is lovely.
40.6: For from thence all the Gods derive beauty, and being filled with it, fill the natures posterior to themselves, exciting all things, agitating them with Bacchic fury about the love of themselves, and pouring supernally on all things the divine effluxion of beauty. — Such therefore, in short, is divine beauty, the supplier of divine hilarity, familiarity and friendship.
40.7: For through this the Gods are united to and rejoice in each other, admire, and are delighted in communicating with each other, and in their mutual replenishings, and do not desert the order which they are always allotted in the distributions of themselves.
40.8: Plato also delivers three indications of this beauty, in the Banquet indeed, denominating it the delicate; for the perfect and that which is most blessed, accedes to the beautiful through the participation of goodness.
40.9: But he this speaks of it in that dialogue: “That which is truly beautiful, is delicate, perfect and most blessed.” One of the indications therefore of the beautiful, is a thing of this kind, viz. the delicate.
40.10: But we may assume another indication of it from the Phædrus, viz. the splendid.
40.11: For Plato attributing this to the beautiful says: “It was then that we were permitted to see splendid beauty shining upon us &c.” And afterwards he adds: “And arriving hither we apprehended it shining most manifestly through the clearest of the senses.” And at last he says: “But now beauty alone has this allotment to be most splendid and most lovely.” These two things therefore are to be assumed as indications of beauty.
40.12: Another indication of beauty is this, that it is the object of love, which now also Plato appears to me to have called most lovely.
40.13: And in many other places he shows that the amatory fury is conversant with the beautiful, defining, and in short, suspending love from the monad of beauty. “For love, says he, is conversant with the beautiful.” Because, therefore, beauty converts and moves all things to itself, causes them to energize enthusiastically, and recalls them through love, it is the object of love, being the leader of the whole amatory series, walking on the extremities of its feet, and exciting all things to itself through desire and astonishment.
40.14: But again because it extends to secondary natures plenitudes from itself, in conjunction with hilarity and divine facility, alluring, enflaming, and elevating all things, and pouring on them illuminations from on high, it is delicate, and is said to be so by Plato.
40.15: And because it bounds this triad, and covers as with a veil the ineffable union of the Gods, swims as it were on the light of forms, causes intelligible light to shine forth, and announces the occult nature of goodness, it is denominated splendid, lucid and manifest.
40.16: For the goodness of the Gods is supreme and most united; their wisdom is in a certain respect now parturient with intelligible light, and the first forms; but their beauty is established in the highest forms, is the luminous precursor of divine light, and is the first thing that is apparent to ascending souls, being more splendid and more lovely to the view and to embrace than every luciferous essence, and when it appears is received with astonishment.
40.17: This triad therefore filling all things, and proceeding through all things, it is certainly necessary that the natures which are filled should be converted to and conjoined with each of the three through kindred, and not through the same media.
40.18: For of different things that are filled by this triad there is a different medium; and different powers are converted to a different perfection of the Gods.
40.19: I think therefore, it is manifest to every one, and it is frequently asserted by Plato, that the cause which congregates all secondary natures to divine beauty, which familiarizes them to it and is the source of their being filled with it, and of their derivation from thence, is nothing else than love, which always conjoins according to the beautiful, secondary to the first Gods, and the more excellent genera, and the best of souls.
40.20: But again, truth is certainly the leader to, and establishes beings in, divine wisdom, with which intellect being filled, possesses a knowledge of beings, and souls participating of this energize intellectually.
40.21: For the full participation of true wisdom is effected through truth, since this every where illuminates intellective natures, and conjoins them with the objects of intellection, just as truth also is the first thing that congregates intellect and the intelligible.
40.22: To those however who hasten to be conjoined with the good, knowledge and co-operation are no longer requisite, but collocation, a firm establishment and quiet are necessary.

41.1: What therefore is it which unites us to the good?
41.2: What is it which causes in us a cessation of energy and motion?
41.3: What is it which establishes all divine natures in the first and ineffable unity of goodness?
41.4: And how does it come to pass that every thing being established in that which is prior to itself according to the good which is in itself, again establishes things posterior to itself according to cause?
41.5: It is, in short, the faith of the Gods, which ineffably unites all the genera of the Gods, of dæmons, and of happy souls to *the good*.
41.6: For it is necessary to investigate *the good* neither gnostically, nor imperfectly, but giving ourselves up to the divine light, and closing the eyes of the soul, after this manner to become established in the unknown and occult unity of beings.
41.7: For such a kind of faith as this is more ancient than the gnostic energy, not in us only, but with the Gods themselves, and according to this all the Gods are united, and about one centre uniformly collect the whole of their powers and progressions. — If however it be requisite to give a particular definition of this faith, let no one suppose that it is such a kind of faith as that which is conversant with the wandering about sensibles.
41.8: For this falls short of science, and much more of the truth of beings.
41.9: But the faith of the Gods surpasses all knowledge, and according to the highest union conjoins secondary with first natures.
41.10: Nor again, let him conceive a faith of a similar species with the celebrated belief in common conceptions; for we believe in common conceptions prior to all reasoning.
41.11: But the knowledge of these is divisible, and is by no means equivalent to divine union; and the science of these is not only posterior to faith, but also to intellectual simplicity.
41.12: For intellect is established beyond all science, both the first science, and that which is posterior to it.
41.13: Neither, therefore, must we say that the energy according to intellect is similar to such a faith as this.
41.14: For intellectual energy is multiform, and is separated from the objects of intellection through difference; and in short, it is intellectual motion about the intelligible.
41.15: But it is necessary that divine faith should be uniform and quiet, being perfectly established in the port of goodness.
41.16: For neither is the beautiful, nor wisdom, nor any thing else among beings, so credible and stable to all things, and so exempt from all ambiguity, divisible apprehension and motion, as *the good*.
41.17: For through this intellect also embraces another union more ancient than intellectual energy, and prior to energy.
41.18: And soul considers the variety of intellect and the splendour of forms as nothing with respect to that transcendency of *the good* by which it surpasses the whole of things.
41.19: And it dismisses indeed intellectual perception, running back to its own hyparxis; but it always pursues, investigates, and aspires after *the good*, hastens as it were to embosom it, and gives itself to this alone among all things without hesitation.
41.20: But why is it necessary to speak of the soul?
41.21: For these mortal animals, as Diotima somewhere says, despise all other things, and even life itself and being, through a desire of the nature of *the good*; and all things have this one immoveable and ineffable tendency to *the good*; but they overlook, consider as secondary, and despise the order of every thing else.
41.22: This, therefore, is the one secure port of all beings.
41.23: This also is especially the object of belief to all beings.
41.24: And through this the conjunction and union with it is denominated faith by theologists, and not by them only, but by Plato likewise, (if I may speak what appears to me to be the case) the alliance of this faith with truth and love is proclaimed in the Laws.
41.25: The multitude therefore are ignorant, that he who has a conception of these things, when discoursing about their contraries, infers the same thing with respect to the deviations from this triad.
41.26: Plato then clearly asserts in the Laws that the lover of falsehood is not to be believed, and that he who is not to be believed is void of friendship.
41.27: Hence it is necessary that the lover of truth should be worthy of belief, and that he who is worthy of belief should be well adapted to friendship.
41.28: From these things therefore, we may survey divine truth, faith and love, and comprehend by a reasoning process their stable communion with each other.
41.29: If, however, you are willing, prior to these things we will recall to our memory that Plato denominates that virtue fidelity which conciliates those that disagree, and subverts the greatest of wars, I mean seditions in cities.
41.30: For from these things faith appears to be the cause of union, communion and quiet.
41.31: And if there is such a power as this in us, it is by a much greater priority in the Gods themselves.
41.32: For as Plato speaks of a certain divine temperance, justice and science, how is it possible that faith which connectedly comprehends the whole order of the virtues should not subsist with the Gods?
41.33: In short, there are these three things which replenish divine natures, and which are the sources of plenitude to all the superior genera of beings, viz. goodness, wisdom and beauty.
41.34: And again, there are three things which collect together the natures that are filled, being secondary indeed to the former, but pervading to all the divine orders, and these are faith, truth and love.
41.35: But all things are saved through these, and are conjoined to their primary causes; some things indeed, through the amatory mania, others through divine philosophy, and others through theurgic power, which is more excellent than all human wisdom, and which comprehends prophetic good, the purifying powers of perfective good, and in short, all such things as are the effects of divine possession.
41.36: Concerning these things therefore, we may perhaps again speak more opportunely.

42.1: Again, let us, if you are willing, from other dialogues investigate the common dogmas of Plato about divine natures.
42.2: Whence therefore, and what dogmas shall we assume, while we proceed in our search according to nature?
42.3: Are you willing that we should in the next place recall to our memory what is written in the Phædo?
42.4: Socrates therefore says in the demonstrations of the immortality of the soul which are derived from its similitude to divinity, that the essence which is superior to the soul, (and to which the soul is naturally similar, and being similar participates of an immortal allotment) is divine and immortal, intelligible and uniform, indissoluble and possesses an invariable sameness of subsistence; but that the essence which is inferior to the soul, is entirely the contrary, to which also it pertains to be corrupted and to be passive.
42.5: For a thing of this kind is sensible and multiform, and is dissoluble because it is a composite; and he predicates among these all such things as pertain to a corporeal subsistence.
42.6: Let us therefore direct our attention to these common dogmas, and examine after what manner each of them pertains to the Gods. — In the first place then what is that which we look to when we speak of that which is said to be divine?
42.7: From what has been said therefore, it is evident that every God subsists according to the highest union of beings.
42.8: For to us ascending from bodies, the Gods have appeared to be superessential unities, the generators, perfectors and measurers of essences, and who bind all first essences to themselves.
42.9: But that which is divine, is not only hyparxis and *the one* in each order of being, but at the same time is that which participates and that which is participated; of which the latter is a God, but the former is divine.
42.10: Whether however, prior to the participated unities, there is something which is separate and participated will be evident in what follows.
42.11: But at present we shall define that which is divine to be a thing of this kind, viz. being which participates of *the one*, or *the one* subsisting contractedly together with being.
42.12: For we assume all things in the Gods except *the one*, as suspended from them and secondary, viz. essence, life and intellect.
42.13: For the Gods do not subsist in, but prior to these, and they produce and contain these in themselves, but are not defined in them.
42.14: But it is necessary not to be ignorant that these are in reality thus distinguished from each other.
42.15: In many places, however, Plato magnificently celebrates the participants of the Gods by the same names, and denominates them Gods.
42.16: For not only the Athenian guest in the Laws calls a divine soul a God, but also Socrates in the Phædrus.
42.17: For he says “that all the horses and charioteers of the Gods are good and consist of things good;” and afterwards still more clearly, “and this is the life of the Gods.” But this is not yet wonderful.
42.18: For is it not admirable that he should denominate those beings Gods who are always conjoined with the Gods, and who together with them give completion to one series?
42.19: For in many places he calls dæmons Gods, though they are essentially posterior to, and subsist about the Gods.
42.20: For in the Phædrus and Timæus, and in other dialogues, you will find him extending the appellation of the Gods even as far as to dæmons.
42.21: But what is still more paradoxical than these things, he does not refuse to call certain men Gods; for in the Sophista he thus denominates the Elean guest.
42.22: From all that has been said therefore, this must be assumed, that with respect to a God, one thing is simply a God, another according to union, another according to participation, another according to contact, and another according to similitude.
42.23: For of superessential natures indeed, each is primarily a God; of intellectual natures, each is a God according to union; and of divine souls, each is a God according to participation.
42.24: But divine dæmons are Gods according to contact with the Gods; and the souls of men are allotted this appellation through similitude.
42.25: Each of these however is, as we have said, rather divine than a God.
42.26: Since the Athenian guest calls intellect itself divine; but that which is divine is posterior to the first deity, in the same manner as that which is united is posterior to *the one*, that which is intellectual, to intellect, and that which is animated, to soul.
42.27: And always those natures that are more uniform and simple have the precedency; but the series of beings ends in *the one itself*.
42.28: Let this, therefore, be the definition and distinction of that which is divine.
42.29: In the next place, let us survey the immortal.
42.30: For with Plato there are many orders of immortality, pervading from on high as far as to the last of things; and the last echo, as it were, of immortality, is in those visible natures that are perpetual; which the Elean guest, in his discourse about the circulation of the universe, says, are allotted from the father a renovated immortality.
42.31: For every body is allotted a being and a life dependent on another cause; but is not itself naturally adapted to connect, or adorn, or preserve itself.
42.32: The immortality of partial souls is, I think, more manifest and more perfect than this; which Plato evinces by many demonstrations in the Phædo, and in the 10th book of the Republic.
42.33: But I mean by the immortality of partial souls, that which has a more principal subsistence, as containing in itself the cause of eternal permanency.
42.34: We shall not, however, err if prior to both these we establish the immortality of dæmons.
42.35: For the genera of these through which they subsist are incorruptible, and they neither verge to mortality, nor are filled with the nature of things which are generated and corrupted.
42.36: But I infer that the immortality of divine souls is still more venerable and essentially more transcendent than that of dæmons; which divine souls we say are primarily self-motive, and are the fountains and principles of the life divided about bodies, and through which bodies obtain a renovated immortality.
42.37: If, however, prior to these you conceive the Gods themselves, and the immortality in them, and how in the Banquet Diotima does not attribute an immortality of this kind even to dæmons, but defines it to subsist in the Gods alone, such an immortality as this will appear to you to be separate, and exempt from the whole of things.
42.38: For there eternity subsists, which is the fountain of all immortality, and through it all things live and possess life, some things indeed a perpetual life, but others a life dispersed into non-being.
42.39: In short, therefore, that which is divine is immortal so far as it generates and comprehends in itself a perpetual life.
42.40: For it is immortal, not as participating of life, but as the supplier of a divine life, and as deifying life itself, whether you are willing to call such a life intelligible, or by any other name.
42.41: In the next place let us direct our attention to the intelligible.
42.42: It is denominated, therefore, in opposition to that which is sensible and which is apprehended by opinion in conjunction with sense.
42.43: For the intelligible is first unfolded into light in the most principal causes.
42.44: For soul is indeed intelligible, is of this allotment, is exempt from sensibles, and obtains an essence separated from them.
42.45: Prior to soul also intellect is intelligible, for we rather think it fit to arrange soul in the middle, than to connumerate it with the first essences.
42.46: That likewise is denominated intelligible, which is more ancient than intellect, which replenishes intelligence, and is itself by itself perfective of it, and which Timæus arranges prior to the demiurgic intellect and intellectual energy, in the order of a paradigm.
42.47: But beyond these is the divine intelligible, which is defined according to union itself, and a divine hyparxis.
42.48: For this is intelligible as the object of desire to intellect, as perfecting and comprehending intellect, and as the plenitude of being.
42.49: In one way, therefore, we must denominate the intelligible as the hyparxis of the Gods; in another way as true being and the first essence; in another way as intellect and all intellectual life; and in another way as soul and the psychical order.
42.50: It is likewise necessary not to fashion the different natures of things conformably to names.
42.51: Such, therefore, is the order of this triad; so that what is divine indeed is unmingled and ranks as the first; that which is immortal is the second; and that which is intelligible the third.
42.52: For the first of these is deified being; the second is life subsisting according to the immortality of the Gods; and the third is intellect, which is denominated intelligible in consequence of being replete with union.

43.1: After this, it follows in the next place, that we should consider the uniform, the indissoluble, and that which has an invariable sameness of subsistence, from the same causes, and these as the precursors of, and pervading through all the divine orders.
43.2: For the uniform, indeed, has the highest subsistence, is present with the divine monad, and appears to be especially adapted to that which is primarily being, and in which also every participable genus of unities ends.
43.3: For *the one* is prior to these, as will be evident as we proceed.
43.4: But the indissoluble is the second.
43.5: For it comprehends and binds the extremes according to divine union; since the dissoluble is such as it is through the want of connexion and of a power which collects multitude into one.
43.6: And that which has an invariable sameness of subsistence is eternal, and is full of the perpetuity of the Gods; from which also the participation of immortality and eternal sameness is derived to other things.
43.7: The uniform, therefore, pertains to the same thing as the divine; but the indissoluble to the same thing as the immortal; and that which has an invariable sameness of subsistence we must refer to the intelligible. — And do you not see how these are severally after a manner co-adapted to each other?
43.8: For the first of these, through the first unity which is participated by being is, as it is fit it should be, uniform.
43.9: For if a God subsists according to *the one*, that which is divine will doubtless be uniform.
43.10: But that which through one cause of life is immortal, is also similarly indissoluble.
43.11: For life is the bond of dissoluble natures; which also Timæus indicating to us, opposes the dissoluble to the immortal: “for you are not immortal, says the demiurgus, yet you shall never be dissolved, nor be subject to the fatality of death.” Every thing mortal, therefore, is dissoluble; but the immortal is indissoluble.
43.12: That, however, which has a renovated immortality is for the same reason neither indissoluble, nor mortal.
43.13: For being in the middle of both it is neither of the extremes, according to each opposition.
43.14: But the third of these being established according to the plenitude of whole intelligibles subsists at once and is invariably the same.
43.15: For the intelligible is the cause of sameness and of eternal permanency; and intellect through this is entirely eternal.
43.16: These triads, therefore, proceed from the first and most principal causes, in the same manner as we demonstrated of the before-mentioned triads.
43.17: But these things, indeed, we shall consider hereafter.
43.18: These things, therefore, being discussed, let us direct our attention to the unbegotten in divine natures, and unfold what we assert it to be.
43.19: For we say that all [true] being is without generation, and Socrates demonstrates in the Phædrus, that souls are unbegotten.
43.20: Prior to these, also, the Gods themselves are established above generations and a subsistence according to time.
43.21: How, therefore, shall we define the unbegotten when applied to a divine nature, and according to what reason?
43.22: Is it because divinity is exempt from all generation, not only from that which subsists in the parts of time, such as we assert the generation of material natures to be, nor from that only which is extended into the whole of time, such as Timæus demonstrates the generation of the celestial bodies to be, but also from the psychical generation?
43.23: Since Timæus denominates this to be unbegotten according to time, but to be the best of generated natures.
43.24: And in short, a divine nature is exempt from all division and essential separation.
43.25: For the progression of the Gods is always according to a union of secondary natures, which are uniformly established in the natures prior to them, the things producing containing in themselves the things produced.
43.26: The indivisible, therefore, the unseparated and the united are in reality unbegotten.
43.27: So that if certain generations of the Gods are spoken of by Plato in fabulous figments, as in the fable of Diotima, the generation of Venus is celebrated, and of Love at the birth of Venus, it is necessary not to be ignorant after what manner things of this kind are asserted, and that they are composed for the sake of symbolical indication; and that fables for the sake of concealment call the ineffable unfolding into light through causes, *generation*.
43.28: For in the Orphic writings, indeed, the first cause is on this account denominated Time; since again, for another reason, it is thus denominated, in order that a subsistence according to cause may be the same as a subsistence according to time.
43.29: And the progression of the Gods from the best of causes is properly denominated generation according to time.
43.30: To Plato, therefore, mythologizing, it is adapted to devise things of this kind conformably to theologists; but when he is discoursing dialectically, and investigating and unfolding divine natures intellectually and not mystically, it is then adapted to him to celebrate the unbegotten essence of the Gods.
43.31: For the Gods primarily establish in themselves the paradigm of non-generation.
43.32: But an intellectual nature is in a secondary degree unbegotten, and after this the psychical essence.
43.33: And in bodies there is an ultimate resemblance of unbegotten power; which some posterior to Plato perceiving, have indefinitely shown that the whole heaven is unbegotten.
43.35: But there is an order in them of first, middle, and last progressions, and a transcendency and subjection of powers.
43.36: There are also in them uniform comprehensions of causes; but multiform progenies of things caused.
43.37: And all things, indeed, are consubsistent in each other; but the mode of subsistence is various.
43.38: For some things as replenishing subsist prior to secondary natures; but others, as being filled aspire after more perfect natures, and participating of their power become generative of things posterior to themselves, and perfective of their hyparxis.

44.1: The most proper beginning however of the theory proposed by us is that from which we may be able to discover the first cause of all beings.
44.2: For being impelled from this in a becoming manner, and having our conceptions purified respecting it, we shall with greater facility be able to distinguish other things.
44.3: About these things therefore we must speak from the beginning as follows: It is necessary that all beings, and all the natures of beings should either be many only, there being no one in them, neither in each, nor in all of them; or that they should be one only, there being no multitude, but all things being compelled into one and the same power of existence; or it is necessary that they should be both one and many, and that being should be one in order that neither multitude itself by itself may vanquish beings, nor that we may be forced to bring together into the same thing all things and their contraries at once.
44.4: These things therefore being three, which of them shall we chuse?
44.5: And to which of the above mentioned assertions shall we give our suffrage.
44.6: It is necessary therefore severally to discuss the absurdities which attend these positions, and thus to survey after what manner the truth subsists. — If then beings are many, and in such a manner many, as we have mentioned from the beginning, so that *the one* is not any where to be found, many absurdities will happen to be the result, or rather all the nature of beings will at once from the first be destroyed, as there will immediately be nothing which is capable of participating *the one*.
44.7: For it must be admitted that every being is either one certain thing, or nothing.
44.8: And that indeed which is a certain being, is also one; but that which is not even one being, has not any existence whatever.
44.9: Hence, if many things have a subsistence, each of the many is something or a certain one.
44.10: But if each of them is nothing, or not even one thing, neither is it possible for the many to exist; for the many are many so far as each individual of the multitude exists.
44.11: If, therefore, the many alone have a subsistence, and *the one* in no respect is, neither will the many exist.
44.12: For things which are in no respect one have not any existence whatever.
44.13: But if *the one* is not, by a much greater priority neither have the many an existence.
44.14: For it necessarily follows that none of the things from which the many consist will have a subsistence.
44.15: Farther still, if the many alone have a subsistence (as has been said) all things will be infinitely infinite; and if you receive any one of the infinites whatever, this also will be immediately infinite.
44.16: And with respect to the things from which this consists and which are infinite, each of these likewise will be infinite.
44.17: For let something of the many be assumed, which we say is not one, this therefore will be multitude according to its own nature, since it belongs to beings, but is not nothing.
44.18: If however it is multitude, this also will consist of many things, and will be many.
44.19: And if you assume something of these manys, this will immediately appear to you not to be one, but many.
44.20: There will likewise be immediately the same reasoning in these, and in a similar manner each, (because we falsely speak of each) will be multitude in energy.
44.21: And each, as I may say, will be infinite, or rather will be infinitely infinite.
44.22: For there is nothing which will not be something of this kind; since a part is many, and in a similar manner the part of a part; and this to infinity.
44.23: For multitude proceeding will never stop, nor infinity, in consequence of being deprived of the nature of *the one*.
44.24: To make beings however, to be infinitely infinite, is impossible both with respect to truth, and to the thing proposed by us.
44.25: For if being is infinitely infinite, being can neither be known, nor discovered; since the infinite is entirely incomprehensible and unknown.
44.26: If also being is infinitely infinite, there will be something more infinite than the infinite.

45.1: But if that something is more infinite, this will be less infinite.
45.2: That, however, which is less infinite; since it is not perfectly infinite, will evidently be finite, so far as it falls short of the nature of the infinite.
45.3: If, therefore, there is something which is itself according to multitude more infinite than that which is infinite in multitude there will be something more than the infinite, and the infinite will be less, yet not according to multitude.
45.5: Hence there is not the infinitely infinite.
45.6: Again therefore, according to this hypothesis, the same things will be according to the same, similar and dissimilar.
45.7: For if all the manys are not one, and each thing according to all things is not one, that which is not one will evidently suffer the same passion in consequence of the privation of *the one*.
45.8: All things therefore being deprived of *the one*, after the same manner, they will on this account subsist similarly with respect to each other.
45.9: But things which subsist similarly, so far as they thus subsist, are evidently similar to each other.
45.10: Hence the many will be similar to each other, so far as they are deprived of *the one*.
45.11: They will likewise according to this privation of *the one* be perfectly dissimilar.
45.12: For it is necessary that things which are similar should suffer the same passion; so that things which do not suffer any thing that is the same, will not be similar.
45.13: But things which suffer any thing that is the same, suffer also one thing.
45.14: Hence things which are deprived of every one, will not suffer any thing that is the same.
45.15: The many therefore will be similar and dissimilar according to the same.
45.17: Hence it is impossible for the many to exist which are in no respect one.
45.18: Moreover, the many will be the same with and different from each other according to the same.
45.19: For if all things are similarly deprived of *the one*, so far indeed as all of them are similarly deprived they will be the same according to this privation; since things which subsist after the same manner according to habit are the same, and also things which are after the same manner deprived according to privation.
45.20: But so far in short, as each of them is deprived of every one, so far the many will be different from each other.
45.21: For if *the one* in the many is the same, that which is in no respect one, will in no respect be the same.
45.22: The many therefore will be the same and not the same with each other.
45.23: But if they are the same and not the same it is evident that they are different from each other.
45.24: For that which is the same and not the same, so far as it is not the same, is not the same, by nothing else than the different.
45.25: Farther still therefore, these many will be moveable and immoveable, if *the one* is not.
45.26: For if each of them is not one, they will be immoveable according to the privation of *the one*.
45.27: For if that which is not one should be changed, each of them would have *the one*; since privations being changed, entirely lead into habits the things that are changed.
45.28: It is necessary however that what is not one should remain immoveable according to the privation of *the one*, though this very thing is itself impossible, viz. that the many should stand still.
45.29: For every thing which stands still is in something which is the same, viz. it is either in the same form, or in the same place.
45.30: But every thing which is in the same, is in one thing which is the same.
45.31: For the same in which it is, is one thing.
45.32: Every thing therefore which stands still is in one thing.
45.33: The many, however, do not participate of *the one*.
45.34: But it is perfectly impossible that things which do not participate of *the one*, should be in one certain thing.
45.35: And things which are not in one thing cannot stand still, since things which stand still are entirely in one and the same thing.
45.36: It is impossible therefore, that the many should stand still, and remain immoveable.

46.1: It has been demonstrated however, that the many must necessarily stand immoveable.
46.2: The same things therefore, and the same passion, (I mean the privation of the habit of *the one*,) are moveable and immoveable.
46.3: For things immoveable, and things which stand still, so far as they are unstable, so far they must necessarily appear to be moveable.
46.4: Moreover, there is no number of beings if *the one* in no respect is; but all things and each thing will be not one.
46.5: For the particle of number, the monad, is one, and every number itself is one.
46.6: For if there are five monads, there is also the pentad; and if three monads, the triad.
46.7: But the triad itself is a certain unity, and so is the pentad.
46.8: So that if there is no one, there will neither be any part, nor the whole of numbers.
46.9: For how can there be any number *the one* not existing?
46.10: For *the one* is the principle of numbers.
46.11: But the principle not existing, neither is it possible that the things which proceed from this principle should exist.
46.12: Hence *the one* not existing, neither will there be any number.
46.13: Again, therefore, neither will there be any knowledge of beings if *the one* is not.
46.14: For it will not be possible either to speak or think of any being.
46.15: For each thing itself, and every thing of which we can speak, and in which we impress the nature of *the one*, will have no existence, because neither does *the one* exist.
46.16: Hence neither will there be any discourse nor any knowledge.
46.17: For discourse is one thing consisting of many things, if it is perfect.
46.18: And knowledge then exists, when that which knows becomes one with that which is known.
46.19: But union not existing, there will at the same time be no knowledge of things, and it will be impossible to speak about things which we know.
46.20: To which we may add, that the inexplicable in the several infinites, will necessarily always fly from the bound of knowledge.
46.21: For immediately each apparent infinite which he who possesses knowledge desires to understand, will escape the gnostic power hastening to come into contact with, and adhere to it, since it is incapable either of contact or adhesion.
46.22: If, therefore, the many alone have an existence, *the one* having no subsistence whatever, so many absurdities, and a still greater number must necessarily happen to those who adopt such an hypothesis.
46.23: But if *the one* which is *the one itself* alone has a subsistence, and there is nothing else (for if there were there would not only be one but many things; since one and another thing are more than one, and are not one thing only) if this be the case, there will neither be among all things either whole, or that which has parts.
46.24: For every thing which has parts is many, and every whole has parts.
46.25: But *the one* is in no respect many.
46.26: Neither therefore will there be a whole, nor that which has parts.
46.27: Farther still, neither is it possible that there should be a beginning, or end of any thing.
46.28: For that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end, is divisible.
46.29: But *the one* is not divisible, because neither has it any parts.
46.30: Hence, neither has it a beginning, nor a middle, nor an end.
46.31: Again, if *the one* alone has a subsistence, no being will have figure.
46.32: For every thing which has figure is either rectilinear or circular, or mixt from these.
46.33: But if indeed it is rectilinear, it will have for its parts, the middle, and the extremes.
46.34: If it is circular, there will be one thing in it as a middle, but other things as extremes, to which the middle extends.
46.35: And if it is mixed from the right and circular line, it will consist of many things, and will not be one.
46.36: Moreover, neither will any being be in itself, nor in another thing.
46.37: For that which is in another thing is different from that in which it is.
46.38: But *the one* alone existing and nothing else (for it will by no means be in another thing) there will be no being which is in another thing.

47.1: But that which is in itself will at the same time comprehend and be comprehended; and in this, to comprehend will not be the same thing as to be comprehended; nor will there be the same definition of both.
47.2: There will therefore be two things, and no longer *the one* alone.
47.3: Again, neither will any being be moved.
47.4: For being moved indeed, it must necessarily be changed.
47.5: But being changed it must be in another thing.
47.6: If *the one* however alone has an existence, it is not possible for any thing to appear to be in something else.
47.7: Hence it is not possible for any being to be changed.
47.8: But every thing which stands still is necessarily in the same thing.
47.9: And that which is in the same is in a certain same thing.
47.10: The one however is in no same thing.
47.11: For that which is in a certain thing, is either in itself, or in something else.
47.12: But it has been demonstrated, that it is neither in itself, nor in another.
47.13: Hence neither is it in a certain same thing.
47.14: Neither therefore does any being stand still.
47.15: Moreover, it is impossible for any thing to be the same with, or different from any thing.
47.16: For if there is nothing besides *the one itself*, there is not any thing which will be either the same with, or different from another thing.
47.17: For there will not be any other being.
47.18: And *the one itself* will not be different from itself; for it would be many and not one.
47.19: Nor will it be the same with itself.
47.20: For this thing which is same is in another, and same is not *the one itself*.
47.21: For *the one* is simply one, because it is not many.
47.22: But that which is same is the same with another thing.
47.23: Again, neither is it possible for any thing to be similar or dissimilar to any thing.
47.24: For every thing similar suffers a certain same passion; but every thing dissimilar a certain different passion. *The one*, however, cannot suffer any thing, nor can this be the case with any thing else besides *the one*; since nothing else has any existence whatever, if *the one* alone has a subsistence.
47.25: Farther still, in addition to these things we say that neither is it possible for any thing to be touched, nor to be separate, if there is nothing else besides *the one*.
47.26: For how can things which have no existence be separate, or come into contact with any thing?
47.27: But neither can *the one* either be separate from itself, or touch itself.
47.28: For it would thus be passive to the being touched, and the being separate.
47.29: But *the one* suffers no other thing besides itself.
47.30: It is likewise requisite that no one thing should either be equal or unequal to any thing.
47.31: For that which is equal to another thing, is said to be so with reference to another thing.
47.32: And the like may be said of that which is unequal.
47.33: Another thing, however, has no existence, if *the one* alone has a subsistence.
47.34: But neither can *the one* be equal or unequal to itself.
47.35: For if unequal, there will be one thing in it as greater, but another as less; so that it will be two things and not one.
47.36: And if *the one* is equal to itself, *the one* will measure itself.
47.38: For *the one* will measure and be measured by itself, so that it will not be *the one itself*.
47.39: Neither therefore will there be any equality or inequality in beings.
47.40: If however these things are impossible, neither can any being come into contact with another, and be separate, nor be similar or dissimilar, nor be same or different, nor again, stand still, or be moved, or in short be in any thing, or have figure, or be a whole, or have parts, if *the one* alone has a subsistence which is void of multitude, and is without all these things.
47.41: Neither however, is it possible for the many alone to have a subsistence, as was before demonstrated.
47.42: And hence it is necessary that every being should be both many and one.

48.1: If this however is the case, either *the many* must participate of *the one*, or *the one* of *the many*, or both must participate of each other, or neither of each other; but *the many* indeed must be separate, and *the one* must also be separate, in order that *the many* and *the one* may subsist, as reason evinces.
48.2: If, therefore, neither *the one* participates of *the many*, nor *the many* of *the one*, the same absurdities will ensue as we brought together in the hypothesis of *the many* alone having a subsistence.
48.3: For again there will be *the many* separate from *the one*.
48.4: For if *the one* subsists by itself, and *the many* do not in any respect participate of *the one*, *the many* will be infinitely infinite, they will be similar and dissimilar, same and different, moved and stable, and there will neither be any number nor any knowledge of *the many*.
48.5: For the absence of *the one* compels all these consequences to be apparent in *the many*.
48.6: It is impossible therefore, that neither *the many* should participate of *the one*, nor *the one* of *the many*.
48.7: If however, *the one* participates of *the many*, and *the many* of *the one*, and both these are in each other, it is necessary that there should be another nature besides these, which is neither one nor many.
48.8: For both these being mingled in each other, it is necessary that there should be a cause of their mixture which conjoins *multitude* to *the one*, and *the one* to *multitude*.
48.9: For it is necessary that every thing that is mingled, should have a cause of the mixture.
48.10: For in short, if *the one* and *multitude* participate of each other, neither *the one* is the cause of essence to *multitude*, nor *multitude* to *the one*, but a certain third thing is the cause of essence to both, and which is prior to these.
48.11: For what will that be which makes this to be multitude, and that to be one?
48.12: And what is the cause of this communication and association with each other, *the one* so far as it is one never having any communication with *the many*?
48.13: For *the many* so far as many, and *the one* so far as one are different from each other.
48.14: And so far as neither is from neither, they have no sympathy with each other.
48.15: What therefore is it which collects these into one, since they fly from and are unmingled with each other?
48.16: For being thus discordant with each other, they cannot desire each other, or if they did their congress must be fortuitous.
48.17: For if this should happen to be the case, there was a time when these were separate from each other, since now also they subsist together causally.
48.18: It is however impossible for *the many* to subsist separate from *the one*.
48.19: The mixture therefore is not causal.
48.20: But neither is the mixture from *the many*, if neither *the one* is the cause of *the many*, nor *the many* of *the one*.
48.21: What therefore is this more excellent thing [which is the cause of the mixture?] For it is either one, or not one.
48.22: But if indeed, it is *the one itself*, we must again inquire concerning this, whether it participates of multitude or of nothing.
48.23: For if this participates, it is evident that some other thing prior to this, will for the same reason present itself to the view, and this will be the case to infinity.
48.24: But if a thing of this kind is entirely void of multitude, again that which was asserted at first will not be true, viz. that *the many* do not participate of *the one*, nor *the one* of *the many*.
48.25: I mean however that which is the most principal and primarily one.
48.26: But there is indeed a certain one in the many, and there is also the imparticipable one, and which is simply one, and nothing else.
48.27: If however that which is prior to both, is *not one*, it is necessary that this *not one* should be more excellent than *the one*.
48.28: All things however are, and are generated what they are, through *the one*.
48.29: And together with *the one* indeed every being is preserved; but separate from *the one* proceeds to the corruption of itself.

49.1: The mixture also of *the one* and *multitude*, which the non-one affords to beings, is communion and union. *The one* therefore, and that which is *not one*, are the cause of nothing else to beings than of their being one.
49.2: If however *the one* is the cause of a thing of this kind, that which is *not one* will not be the cause of that which is more excellent [than union.] But it is every where necessary that what is more excellent should be the cause to beings of another more excellent thing, according to its own power.
49.3: For thus it will be more excellent as being more good, and as the cause from its own nature of a greater and more excellent good to those things to which a less good is the cause of less goodness.
49.4: From these things therefore it is necessary, that *the many* should participate of *the one*, that *the one* should be unmingled with *multitude*, and that nothing should be better than *the one*, but that this should also be the cause of being to *the many*.
49.5: For every thing which is deprived of *the one*, flies immediately into nothing, and to its own corruption.
49.6: But that which is not many, is not at one and the same time not many and nothing.
49.7: For to *the one* that which is nothing, or not one, is opposed, and to *the many* that which is not many is opposed.
49.8: If, therefore, *the one* and *the many* are not the same, the not being many will not be the same with nothing.
49.9: From thus considering the affair therefore, it appears that *the one* is beyond multitude, and is the cause of being to *the many*.

50.1: It is necessary however, that discussing the same subject after another manner, we should again see if we can in a certain respect follow what has been said, and refer it to the same end.
50.2: It is necessary therefore, that there should either be one principle, or many principles; or rather, we should begin from hence.
50.3: And if there are many principles, they must either possess sympathy with each other, or they must be divulsed from each other, and they must be either finite or infinite.
50.4: But if there is one principle, this must either be not essence, or essence.
50.5: And if it is essence, this must either be corporeal or incorporeal.
50.6: And if incorporeal, it must either be separate from, or inseparable from bodies.
50.7: And if separate, it must either be moveable or immoveable.
50.8: But if it is not essence, it must either be inferior to all essence, or participated by essence, or imparticipable.
50.9: If therefore there are many principles, and which have no sympathy with each other, no being will originate from them [conjointly,] nor will they be common to all things, but each will produce by itself.
50.10: For what communication can there be between things which are naturally foreign, or what co-operation between things which are entirely of a different kind?
50.11: In addition also to these things, there will be *the many* which do not participate of *the one*.
50.12: For if there is a certain one common in all of them, they will not be perfectly separated essentially from each other.
50.13: If therefore they are different, and there is nothing which is the same about them, they are alone many and by no means one.
50.14: But if there are many principles, and which possess sympathy with each other, they will have something common, which leads all of them to sympathy, and similarly unfolds all of them to the view.
50.15: For we call those things sympathetic, which happen to be passive to the same thing.
50.16: But similars are entirely similar from participating one form and one nature.
50.17: If however this be the case, it is necessary that that all [or universal] which is every where, and in all the principles, should be of a more principal nature than the many.
50.18: This therefore gives them the power to generate sympathy with each other, and affords them communion according to nature. — Again, if there are indeed infinite principles, either the things which proceed from them are infinite, and there will thus be the infinite twice, or they are finite, and thus all the principles will not be principles.
50.19: For things finite in number, will entirely proceed from finite principles.
50.20: The principles therefore are in vain infinite.
50.21: To which may be added, that infinity makes both the principles to be unknown, and the things which proceed from them.
50.22: For the principles being unknown, it is necessary that the things which proceed from them should be unknown; since we then think that we know any thing when we know the causes and the first principles of it.
50.23: But if the principles are finite, it is evident that there will be a certain number of them: for we say that number is a definite multitude.
50.24: If however, there is a number of the principles, it is necessary that there should be a cause of the whole number of them.
50.25: For every number is from one; and this, viz. *the one* is the principle of numbers.
50.26: This therefore will be the principle of principles, and the cause of finite multitude, since number itself is one, and the end in the many is one, and it bounds the many by that which is one.
50.27: But the principle being one, and this being essence, it is necessary if this is admitted to be either corporeal or incorporeal, that it must be acknowledged to be the principle of other things.
50.28: If therefore, body is the cause of the generation of beings, it is necessary indeed, that it should be divisible and have parts.
50.29: For every body is in its own nature divisible; since every magnitude is a certain whole and that which is a whole consists of parts.

51.1: These parts therefore, (but I mean each of them) must either severally participate a certain one, or not participate it.
51.2: If therefore they do not participate it, they will be many alone, and by no means one.
51.3: Hence, neither will that which consists from them be a whole.
51.4: For there being no one, that which consists of all of them will not be one.
51.5: But if each of the parts participates of something of this kind, and there is something which is the same in all of them, a thing of this kind must necessarily be incorporeal, and impartible according to its own nature.
51.6: For if this also is itself corporeal, it is either wholly in each of the parts, or not wholly.
51.7: If therefore, it is indeed wholly in each, it will itself be separated from itself.
51.8: For the parts in which it is are separate from each other.
51.9: But if it is not wholly in each of the parts, this also will be divisible, and will have parts after the same manner as the above mentioned parts; and there will again be the same inquiry concerning these, viz. whether in these also there is something common, or nothing; since if there is nothing common, we shall place *the many* separate from *the one*.
51.10: Let us however consider the whole; for every body is a whole, and has parts.
51.11: What therefore will that be which is connective of the parts, since they are many?
51.12: For it is necessary to say either that the whole is unific of the parts, or the parts of the whole, or that some third thing prior to both, which is neither a whole, nor has any part, connects and unites the whole with its parts, and the parts with the whole.
51.13: But if the whole indeed is connective of the parts, the whole will be incorporeal and impartible.
51.14: For if it is a body, this also will be partible, and will be indigent of a nature which is capable of connecting the parts; and this will be the case to infinity.
51.15: But if the parts are connective of the whole, how can *the many* be connective of *the one*; and things divided, of that which consists from them?
51.16: For on the contrary, it is necessary that *the one* should have the power of uniting *the many*, and not *the many* of uniting *the one*.
51.17: And if that which connects both, is neither a whole nor has parts, it will be perfectly impartible.
51.18: But being impartible, it is also necessarily without interval.
51.19: For every thing which has interval has parts, and is divisible.
51.20: But being without interval it is incorporeal; for every body possesses interval.
51.21: Farther still, it is necessary that the principle should be perpetual; for every being is perpetual or corruptible.
51.22: Hence it must be admitted that the principle of beings is perpetual or corruptible.
51.23: But if we should grant that this may be corrupted, there will be no being incorruptible.
51.24: For the principle being destroyed, it will neither be itself generated from any thing, nor will another thing be generated from it.
51.25: For it can neither be able to generate itself (since it is not, if it is not perpetual) nor can another thing be able to generate it, if it is the principle of all things.
51.26: But if it is incorruptible, it will have the power of not being corrupted, and this power will be infinite, in order that it may exist to infinity through the whole of time.
51.27: For every finite power of existence pertains naturally to that which is corruptible.
51.28: But an infinite power pertains to perpetual natures, the existence of which continues to infinity.
51.29: This infinite therefore, I mean the infinite according to power, is either impartible or partible.
51.30: But if it is partible indeed, there will be the infinite in a finite body.
51.31: For the principle is finite; since if it were infinite, there will be nothing else besides itself.
51.32: But if it is impartible, the power of infinitely existing will be incorporeal.
51.33: And the principle of beings is incorporeal, so far as it is this power through which the subject of it always is.
51.34: That it is impossible therefore, the principle of beings can be corporeal is from these things evident.

52.1: If however it is incorporeal, it must either be separate, or inseparable from bodies.
52.2: But if inseparable indeed, it will have all its energies in bodies, and subsisting about them.
52.3: For that is inseparable from body which is not any where naturally adapted to energize except in and with bodies.
52.4: But if the principle is a thing of this kind, it is evidently necessary that none of the things which subsist according to it should be more powerful, or possess greater authority than the principle of all beings.
52.5: If however, nothing is more excellent in bodies than the power which subsists in and energizes about bodies, and a corporeal essence, there will not any where be intellect and the power which energizes according to intellect.
52.6: For every such like motion [i.e. energy] proceeds from a power, which is entirely in its energies independent of body.
52.7: But it neither was, nor is lawful for generated natures to surpass the power of their causes.
52.8: For every thing which is in the things begotten is from primary natures, and the latter are the lords of the essence of the former.
52.9: If therefore, the principle of beings is able to generate intellect and wisdom, how is it possible it should not generate it, on account of and in itself?
52.10: For one of two things is necessary, either that intellectual perception pertains in no respect to beings, or that it is inferior to them; and that if it exists it acts in bodies only.
52.11: These things however, it is impossible to assert.
52.12: But if that which is the first of beings, and which is the principle of all things is separate from bodies, it is perfectly necessary to admit that it is either immoveable or moved.
52.13: And if indeed it is moved, there will be something else prior to it, about which it is moved.
52.14: For every thing which is moved, is naturally adapted to be moved about something else which is permanent.
52.15: And farther still, besides this, it is moved through desire of another thing.
52.16: For it is necessary indeed that it should be moved in consequence of desiring a certain thing; because motion itself by itself is indefinite.
52.17: But the end of it is that for the sake of which it subsists.
52.18: It desires however, either something else, or itself.
52.19: But every thing which desires itself is immoveable.
52.20: For why should any thing that is present with itself want to be in another thing?
52.21: For of things which are moved, the motion of that is less to which the good is nearer, but the motion is greater of that to which the good is more remote.
52.22: But that which possesses good in itself, and for the sake of which it subsists, will be immoveable and stable; since being always in itself, it is in good.
52.23: That however which is in itself is in same; for each thing is the same with itself.
52.24: But of that which is in itself we say indeed that it stands still and is immoveable; while that which is not immoveable, is not in itself but in another, is moved towards another thing, and is perfectly indigent of good.
52.25: If therefore the principle of beings is moved, but every thing which is moved is moved through the want of good, and towards another thing which is the object of desire to it, there will be something else which is desirable to the principle of beings besides itself, and about which possessing a sameness of subsistence, we must say it is moved.
52.27: For the principle is that for the sake of which all things subsist, which all things desire, and which is indigent of nothing.
52.28: For if it were in want of something, it would be entirely subordinate to that of which it is in want, and to which its energy is directed as the object of desire.
52.29: But if the principle is immoveable (for this is what remains,) it is necessary that it should be one incorporeal essence, possessing an eternal sameness of subsistence.
52.30: After what manner, however, does it possess *the one*?
52.31: And how is it one essence?
52.32: For if essence and *the one* are the same, it must be admitted that the principle of beings is essence.

53.1: But if essence is different from *the one*, it must be granted that to be *the one* is not the same thing as to be essence.
53.2: And if, indeed, essence is better than *the one*, according to this it must be said to be with the principle.
53.3: But if *the one* is better than essence and beyond it, *the one* is also the principle of essence.
53.4: And if they are coordinate to each other, the many will be prior to *the one*.
53.5: This, however, is impossible as we have before demonstrated.
53.6: It is evident, indeed, that essence is not the same as *the one*.
53.7: For it is not one and the same thing to say one, and that essence is one; but the former is not yet a sentence, and the latter is.
53.8: To which may be added, that if essence and *the one* are the same, multitude will be the same as that which has no existence, and which is not essence.
53.10: For in essence the many are contained, and in that which is not essence is *the one*.
53.11: But if essence and *the one* are not the same, they will not be coordinate to each other; for if they were coordinate there will be some other thing prior to them, if it is necessary that all things should subsist from one principle.
53.12: And if one of these is better than the other, either *the one* is prior to essence, or essence is prior to *the one*.
53.13: But if *the one* indeed is prior to essence, this and not essence is the principle of all things.
53.14: For it is necessary that nothing should be better than the principle.
53.15: And if essence is prior to *the one*, *the one* will be passive to essence, and not essence to *the one*.
53.16: But if *the one* is passive to essence, it is necessary that *the one* and essence should be every thing, and that all such things as are one should be essence, but not that all such things as are essence should be one.
53.17: There will, therefore, be a certain essence deprived of *the one*.
53.18: If, however, this be the case, it will be nothing.
53.19: For that which is deprived of *the one* is nothing.
53.20: Hence *the one* is prior to essence.
53.21: But if that which is first is something which is not essence, it is absurd to assert that it is subordinate to essence.
53.22: For the principle is that which has the greatest power and the most absolute authority, and is most sufficient to itself, and is not that which is most ignoble, and indigent of the many.
53.23: And, in short, it is necessary that no secondary nature should be better than the principle; for it is requisite that beings should not be governed badly.
53.24: But if, indeed, the principle has an order subordinate to the things which proceed from it, and the things proceeding from it are better than it, all things will be badly confounded, nor will the principle according to nature be any thing else than something which is not the most excellent of things, nor will things which proceed from the principle possess from it a power of ruling over their principle.
53.25: The principle of beings, therefore, will indeed be fortuitous, and also the beings which are its progeny.
53.27: For things which are fortuitous (if to have a fortuitous subsistence is this, not to exist according to intellect, nor with a view to a definite end) are disorderly, infinite, and indefinite, and are all of them things which have a less frequency of subsistence.
53.28: But the principle is invariably principle, and other things proceed from it.
53.29: If however, that which is not essence is better than all essence, it will either be participated by it, or it will be entirely imparticipable.
53.30: If, however, essence participates of the principle, of what will it be the principle?
53.31: And how will it be the principle of all beings?
53.32: For it is necessary that the principle of beings should be no one of beings; since if it were any one of them, it is necessarily not the principle of all beings.
53.33: But every thing which is participated by another thing is said to be that by which it is participated, and in which it primarily is.

54.1: The principle, however, is separate, and belongs in a greater degree to itself than to other things.
54.2: Besides, every thing which is participated proceeds from another more excellent cause; since that which is imparticipable is better than that which is participable.
54.3: It is not, however, possible to conceive any thing better than that which is most excellent, and which we call the principle.
54.4: For it is not lawful to assert that things secondary to the principle, and which proceed from it, are in any respect better than their principle.
54.5: The cause therefore of all beings is above all essence, is separate from every essence, and is neither essence, nor has essence as an addition to its nature.
54.6: For such an addition as this is a diminution of simplicity, and of that which is one.

55.1: See, therefore, the third argument after these, leading us to the same conclusion with the former arguments.
55.2: For it is necessary that the cause of all beings should be that of which all beings participate, to which they refer the subsistence of themselves, and which separates itself from nothing that in any respect whatever is said to have an existence.
55.3: For this alone is the object of desire to beings, which primarily, or in some other way, is itself the cause of their subsistence.
55.4: And it is necessary that every thing which is produced with reference to, and on account of it, should have a certain habitude with relation to it, and through this also, a similitude to it.
55.5: For every habitude of one thing towards another, is predicated in a twofold respect, either from both participating of one thing, which affords to the participants a communion with each other; or from one of them participating of the other; of which, indeed, the one as being more excellent, imparts something to that which is subordinate to itself; but the other, as being inferior, is assimilated to the more excellent nature, so far as it participates of it.
55.6: Hence it is necessary, if all sensible natures possess a habitude to that which is first, aspire after, and subsist about it, either that there should be a certain third thing the cause of the habitude, or that the principle should impart to the natures posterior to itself, a tendency to itself, and that desire, through which every thing is preserved, and exists.
55.7: Nothing else, however, is more excellent than that which is first.
55.8: Hence, the habitude of beings, their existence, and their tendency to the first, are derived from thence.
55.9: And all things participate of the principle of themselves, if it is necessary that this which is participated, should from thence become apparent in all beings, since it is the principle of all things, and deserts no being whatever.
55.10: What, therefore, will this nature be, which is every where, and in all beings?
55.12: But there are indeed many things which are deprived of these.
55.13: Is, therefore, permanency every where, and in all things?
55.15: For motion, so far as it is motion, will not participate of permanency.
55.16: Is much-honoured intellect, therefore, so far as it is intellect, participated by all beings?
55.18: For all beings would have intellectual perception, and no being would be deprived of intellect. — Shall we say, therefore, that being itself and essence are participated by all things that in any respect whatever have a subsistence?
55.20: For that which is in generation, or passing into existence, is said to be, and is destitute of essence.
55.21: Nor must we wonder, if it also, since it ranks among beings, should now participate of essence.
55.22: For so far as it is in generation, it is not; but it ends in existence and essence when it is now actually generated, and is no longer rising into existence.
55.23: All things, therefore, that have in any respect whatever a subsistence, do not participate of essence.
55.24: What then will that be which is every where and by all things participated?
55.25: Let us consider every being, and see what that is to which all beings are passive, and what it is which is common in all of them, as in essence, sameness, difference, permanency, and motion.
55.26: Can we say, therefore, that each of these is any thing else than one thing, and not only separately, but this is also the case with the things which subsist from them; and in short, it is not possible in a certain respect to speak otherwise of all things, than this, that all things, and each thing is one.
55.27: For if any thing should be deprived of *the one*, though you should speak of parts, or of beings, immediately, that which becomes destitute of *the one*, will be altogether nothing.

56.1: Or with what intention do we say that a thing which is not is perfectly nothing, [or not even one thing] unless *the one* is the last thing which deserts beings?
56.2: This it is, therefore, to become that which in no respect is, and to be perfectly deprived of *the one*.
56.3: For it is possible for that which is not moved to be, and for that which has no being to have an hyparxis; but that which is not even one thing, and which is destitute of *the one itself*, will be entirely nothing.
56.4: Hence *the one* is present with all beings; and though you should speak of multitude itself, it is necessary that this also should participate of *the one*; for if it does not become one thing, it is not possible for it to subsist.
56.5: And if even you divide the whole to infinity, immediately nothing else than one occurs.
56.6: For either that which is divided does not subsist, or becoming to be, or subsisting something else, it will be immediately one. *The one*, therefore, which is every where apparent, and is in all beings, and which deserts no being whatever, is either derived from *the one* which is simply one, or from that which is more excellent than *the one*.
56.7: For it is not possible for *the one* to be otherwise passive, [i.e. to be consubsistent with something else] than from the first one, to which *the one* is no longer present, but which is *the one itself*, or nothing else than one.
56.8: Again, therefore, from another principle we may arrive at the same conclusion, by speaking as follows: It is necessary either that the causes of beings and things caused should proceed to infinity, and that there should be nothing first or last in beings; or that there should be no first, but that there should be the last of things, infinity existing in one part only.
56.9: Or on the contrary, it is necessary that beings should proceed to infinity from a definite principle, or that there should be a certain first and last, and a boundary of beings each way.
56.10: And if there are boundaries of beings, things either proceed from each other, and the generation of beings is in a circle; or if they are not from each other, either one of them is from another, or the first indeed is one, but the last not one, or the contrary, or both are one, or each is not one.
56.11: If, therefore, first things, and the causes of beings are infinite, each thing will consist of infinites.
56.12: For that which proceeds from a certain principle, must necessarily participate of that principle from which it proceeds.
56.13: But that which derives its subsistence from many causes, will be in its own nature multiform, as participating of many powers.
56.14: And that which is produced from infinites prior to itself, will have infinite peculiarities derived from the principles, and adapted to itself.
56.15: Every being, therefore, being infinite, and consisting of infinites, will render all things infinitely infinite, and there will neither be a knowledge of any being, nor any evolution of powers.
56.16: For the power of the infinite is perfectly unknown, and incomprehensible, by those natures to whom it is infinite.
56.17: But if things are infinite in a descending progression, whether is each of them infinite always proceeding most downward, in the same manner as we say all things do, or is each whole indeed finite, but the beings which are produced from these are infinite?
