181.47: For the parts of this wholeness, are more partial powers, which hasten indeed to a progression from the father, but are on all sides established and comprehended by the wholeness.
181.48: And the wholeness itself is a deity, connectedly containing in itself intelligible parts, being parturient indeed with intellectual multitude, generating all things stably, and again embosoming and collecting to itself its progeny, and as the more tragical fables say, absorbing and depositing them in itself.
181.49: For the progeny of it are twofold; some indeed, being, as it were, analyzed into it; but others being divided from it.
181.50: And some abiding in it through the first unpolluted monad; but others proceeding according to the prolific cause of the intellectual Gods, surmounting the union of the father, and being the primary leaders of another order, and of the arrangement and ornament of secondary natures.
181.51: The first order therefore of the intellectual Gods, is thus delivered to us by Parmenides.

182.1: The second order however, after this, is that which comprehends the middle genera of wholes, is the cause to all things of progression and prolific power, and is in continuity with the first order of the intellectual Gods.
182.2: What else therefore than life is every where in continuity with the intelligible and true being?
182.3: For it is the medium between intellect and the intelligible, conjoining intellect to the intelligible, and expressing the intelligible power which collects together *the one* and being.
182.4: As the intelligible therefore is to *the one* and hyparxis, so is life to power, and intellect to being.
182.5: And as in intelligibles, *the one* is the object of desire, but being aspires after the participation of *the one*, and power collects being to the participation of *the one*, and *the one* to a communion with being, (for *the one* here is not imparticipable, and exempt from all power) so likewise the intelligible is the object of desire to intellect, but intellect is filled with it.
182.6: And life binds indeed intellect to the intelligible, but unfolds the intelligible to intellect.
182.7: Whence also, I think, those who are wise in all divine concerns, call *the one* and hyparxis intelligible.
182.8: But that which is primarily being, they call the first intellect, conformably to this analogy.
182.9: Life therefore, is the medium between being and intellect, in the same manner as power subsists between *the one* and being.
182.10: And all these, viz. the intelligible, life, and intellect are primarily in intelligibles; but secondarily in intelligibles and intellectuals; and according to a third diminution, in intellectuals.
182.11: In intelligibles however, being is according to essence; for there intellect is primarily according to cause.
182.12: But in intellectuals, intellect indeed, is according to essence; but the natures prior to intellect, are according to participation.
182.13: Since therefore, life is surveyed in a threefold respect, in intelligibles indeed according to cause; but in intelligibles and intellectuals, according to hyparxis; and an intellectuals, according to participation, it is indeed necessary that the life which is in the intellectual order, should both be life, and participate of the causes generative of life prior of itself. *The one* therefore of the intellectual Gods which is arranged in the middle, is not motion, but that which is moved.
182.14: For prior to this, it has been demonstrated by Plato, that all life is motion.
182.15: For soul is self-motive because it is self-vital.
182.16: And intellect is on this account moved, because it has the most excellent life.
182.17: The first vivific cause, therefore, of the intellectual Gods, is primarily allotted motion.
182.18: If, however, it was the first-effective and highest life, it would be requisite to denominate it motion, and not that which is moved.
182.19: But since it is life as in intellectuals, but is filled from exempt life, it is at the same time motion, and that which is moved.
182.20: Very properly, therefore, does Parmenides demonstrate that *the one* in this order is moved, because it proceeds from the causes of all life that are placed above it, and is analogous to the middle centre of intelligibles, and to the middle triad of intelligibles and intellectuals.
182.21: Hence also, Socrates in the Phædrus calls this middle triad Heaven; for the whole of it is life and motion.
182.22: But that which is moved, is the middle in intellectuals, as being filled from it, [i.e. from the life in the middle triad of intelligibles and intellectuals;] since eternity also, which is arranged according to the intelligible wholeness, is all-perfect life, and all life, according to Plotinus.
182.23: There, however, the middle is life according to cause; but in intellectuals, it is life according to participation; and in the order between these, it is life according to essence, proceeding indeed from intelligible life, (as Parmenides also manifests, characterizing both according to wholeness, though the wholeness in intelligibles is different from that which is in intelligibles and intellectuals, as we have before observed,) but producing after this, intellectual life.
182.24: For that which is moved, is indeed entirely allied to the circulation of the Heaven, and to intellectual and intelligible life. — Moreover, the permanency which is coordinate with this motion, is not one certain genus of being, as neither is motion.
182.25: For beings indeed are naturally adapted to participate of the genera of being; but the superessential goods of the Gods, are expanded above the order of beings.
182.26: If, therefore, Parmenides here, assuming *the one itself* by itself, surveys in this motion and permanency, he evidently does net attribute the elements of being to the Gods, but assigns to them peculiarities appropriate, all-perfect, and transcending wholes.
182.27: And thus asserting that *the one* is moved and stands still, according to motion, indeed, he delivers the vivific hyparxis of the Gods, the generative fountain of wholes, and the leading cause of all things.
182.28: But according to permanency, he delivers the unpolluted monad coordinated with motion, and which connectedly-contains the middle centres of the guardian triad.
182.29: For as the summit of the guardian triad, is united to the first father, according to the first hypostasis, thus also the deity who contains the middle bond of the unpolluted leaders, is by a congeniality of nature consubsistent with the motive cause of all the Gods, which moves wholes, and is primarily moved from itself.
182.30: And through this deity, the prolific power of this Goddess [Rhea] is firmly established in herself.
182.31: Producing likewise, and multiplying all things, she is [through this deity] exempt from wholes, and inflexibly exists prior to her progeny.
182.32: With respect, therefore, to motion here and permanency, the former indeed is the fountain of the life and generative power that proceeds to all things; but the latter, establishes the whole vivific fountain in itself, but is from thence filled with the prolific rivers of life.
182.33: Parmenides, therefore, delivering to us these things, and the progression of them, demonstrates that that which is moved is generated from that which is in another, but that which stands still, from that which is in itself.
182.34: For the first monad of the paternal triad constitutes the natures posterior to it.
182.35: And after the same manner, the highest of the unpolluted triad, and which is intelligible as in this triad, imparts at one and the same time the middle and last monad of the triad.
182.36: On this account, also, motion here is better than permanency.
182.37: For as a subsistence in another is according to cause more ancient than the subsistence of a thing in itself, so likewise that which is moved, is causally more ancient than that which is permanent.
182.38: For the unpolluted Gods, are in power subordinate to the fathers, and are comprehended in them.

183.1: The third, therefore, to the Saviour, as they say, and let us direct our attention to the demiurgic monad, unfolding itself into light together with the coordinate Gods it contains.
183.2: In the first place, then, here also the communion of *the one* with other things is apparent, and we must no longer consider *the one* alone by itself, but according to its habitude towards other things.
183.3: Because, therefore, the demiurgic order produces wholes from itself, and arranges and adorns a corporeal nature, it also generates all the second and ministrant causes of the Gods.
183.4: For what occasion is there to say that the term *other things*, is a sign of a corporeal condition of being, since formerly the Pythagoreans thought fit to characterize an incorporeal nature by *the one*, but indicated to us the nature which is divisible about body, through the term *others*?
183.5: In the second place, the number of the conclusions [in this part of the Parmenides] is doubled.
183.6: For *the one* is no longer demonstrated to be alone same, or different, as it is to be in itself, and in another, or to be moved, and stand still, but it is demonstrated to be the same with itself, and different from itself, and to be different from other things, and the same with other things.
183.7: But this twice appeared to us before to be entirely adapted to the demiurgic monad, both according to other theologists, and to Socrates in the Cratylus, who says that the demiurgic name is composed from two words.
183.8: In the third place, therefore, the multitude of causes is here separated, and all the monads of the Gods present themselves to the view, according to the demiurgic progression.
183.9: For the demiurgic order is apparent, the prolific power coordinate with it, the undefiled monad the cause of exempt providence, and the distributive fountain of wholes; and together with these, as I may say, all the orders about the demiurgus are apparent, according to which he produces and preserves all things, and being exempt from the things produced, is firmly established in himself, and separates his own kingdom, from the united empire of his father. — How, therefore, and through what particulars do these things become apparent?
183.10: We reply, that *the same with itself* (for this Parmenides first demonstrates) represents to us about the nature of *the one*, the monadic and paternal peculiarity, according to which the demiurgus also subsists.
183.11: Hence, likewise, *the one* is said to be the same with itself.
183.12: For *the another* is in the demiurgus according to the transcendency of different causes; but *the same*, appears to be a sign of his proper, viz. of his paternal, hyparxis.
183.13: For being one, and the exempt father and demiurgus of wholes, he establishes his proper union in himself.
183.14: And in this one, Parmenides in a remarkable manner shows the uniform, and that which is allied to bound.
183.15: But *the same with other things*, is the singular good of prolific power, and of a cause proceeding to, and pervading through all things without impediment.
183.16: For the demiurgus is present to all things which he produces, and is in all things the same, which he arranges and adorns, pre-establishing in himself the generative essence of wholes.
183.17: If, therefore, we rightly assert these things, bound and infinity subsist in him demiurgically.
183.18: And the one indeed is in the sameness which is separate from other things, but the other is in the power which generates other things.
183.19: For every where power is prolific of secondary natures.
183.20: But the principle which subsists according to bound, is the supplier of an united and stable hypostasis.
183.21: Moreover, *the different from other things*, manifests his undefiled purity, and his transcendency which is exempt from all secondary natures.
183.22: For the first intellect was on this account pure and incorruptible, as Socrates says in the Cratylus, because it is established above coordination or communion with all sensible natures.
183.23: For as some one of the Gods says, he does not incline his power to matter, but is at once exempt from all fabrication.
183.24: But the demiurgic intellect receiving from thence total power, and a royal dominion, adorns indeed sensibles, and constitutes the whole of a corporeal nature.
183.25: Together however, with prolific abundance, and the providential attention to secondary natures, he transcends his progeny, and abides in his own accustomed manner, as Timæus says, through the inflexible guard which subsists with him, and the power imparted to him from it, which is uncontaminated with other participants.
183.26: Hence, through the never-failing supply of good, and providential energies, and the generation of subordinate natures, he is *the same with them*.
183.27: For he is participated by them, and fills his progeny with his own providential care.
183.28: But through his purity, undefiled power, and inflexible energies, he is separate from wholes, is disjoined from them, and is imparticipable by other things.
183.29: And as the first king of intellectuals is allotted his non-inclination to matter, through the guard which is united to him, and through the undefiled monad; and as the vivific goddess possesses her stable and inflexible power from the second cause of the guardian Gods; thus also the demiurgic intellect preserves a transcendency exempt from other things, and a union separated from multitude, through the third monad of the leaders of purity.

184.1: For the cause of separate providence is a guard coordinate with the demiurgus, who hastens to produce all things, and to pervade through all things.
184.2: But the guard which is the supplier of stable power, is coordinate with the vivific deity, who is moved to the generation of wholes.
184.3: And with the intellect that is multiplied according to intellectual conceptions [i.e. with Saturn,] the guard is coordinate, that imparts an undefiled union of the conversion of all his energies to himself.
184.4: The monad, therefore, remains, which is arranged as the seventh of these intellectual monads, which is present with, and energizes with all of them, but particularly unfolds itself into light in the demiurgic order, and which Parmenides also producing for us together with the whole demiurgus, defines it in *difference*, in the same manner as he does the undefiled cause in the demiurgus.
184.5: He says however, that this difference separates the demiurgic monad itself from itself.
184.6: For we have before observed that this order is the supplier of separation to all the Gods.
184.7: As therefore, the demiurgus is the same with himself, through the paternal union, after the same manner he is separated from himself and his father through this difference.
184.8: Whence therefore, does he derive this power?
184.9: From being in himself, says Parmenides, and in another.
184.10: For these were indeed unitedly in the first father, but separately in the third.
184.11: Separation therefore, pre-existed there according to cause; but in the demiurgus it shines forth, and unfolds the power of itself.
184.12: That the cause however of division, is in a certain respect in the first father, Parmenides manifests in the first hypothesis, when he says, “that every thing which is in itself is in a certain respect a duad, and is separated from itself.” There however, the duad is occultly; but here it subsists more clearly, where also all intellectual multitude shines forth to the view.
184.13: For difference is the progeny of the firmly-abiding duad which is there.
184.14: This therefore separates the demiurgic intellect from the Gods prior to it, and divides the monads in it from each other.
184.15: For if so far as it is in another, it is united to the intelligible of itself, but so far as it is in itself it is separated from it, because it proceeds according to each order of its own intelligible,--if this be the case, it is necessary that this difference should be the cause to it of separation from its father.
184.16: All the intellectual monads therefore, have appeared to us to subsist coordinately with each other.
184.17: And the subsistence indeed, *in another* is the sign of the father.
184.18: But the subsistence *in itself*, is the sign of the first unpolluted monad.
184.19: Again, *motion* is the sign of vivific goodness; but *permanency* of the inflexible power conjoined with motion.
184.20: And *sameness with itself, and with another*, is the sign of the demiurgic peculiarity; but the being *different from other things*, is the sign of the guard about the demiurgus.
184.21: And in the last place, *the being different from itself*, is the sign of the seventh intellectual monad, which is according to cause indeed, and occultly in the first father, but is allotted its hypostasis more clearly in the demiurgus.
184.22: Parmenides likewise appears to me, when dividing the signs of fabrication, to have unfolded in the middles themselves, the peculiarities of the undefiled monad, and of the dividing monad, so far as they also are in a certain respect comprehended in the fabrication.
184.23: For he shows in the first of the conclusions that *the one* is *the same with itself*; in the second, that it is *different from itself*; in the third, that it is *different from other things*; and in the fourth that it is *the same with other things*.
184.24: For he co-arranges indeed, the dividing power with the paternal union; but connects with a transcendency separate from secondary natures, the providential cause of them.
184.25: For in the Gods, it is necessary that union should exist prior to separation, and a purity unmingled with secondary natures, prior to a providential inspection of them; through which likewise, being every where, they are no where, being present with all things, they are exempt from all things, and being all things, they are not any of their progeny. i.e.

184.31: Synesius does not here speak conformably to the Chaldean theologists, from whom he has derived these appellations.

184.33: Both these orders therefore, are superior to the angelic series.

185.1: This unscientific manner however of calling both the highest and lowest divine powers by the common name of angels, is not peculiar to Synesius and the Jews, but to all the fathers of the church, and all the Christian divines that succeeded them.
185.2: Gregory, in the 70th proposition of, the first book of his Elements of Astronomy, says of Kepler, “That his archetypal ratios, geometrical concinnities, and harmonic proportions, show such a force of genius as is not to be found in any of the writers of physical astronomy before him.
185.3: So that Jeremiah Horrox, a very competent judge of these matters, though a little averse to Kepler, in the beginning of his astronomical studies, after having in vain tried others, entirely falling in with Kepler’s doctrine and physical reasons, thus addresses his reader: Kepler is a person whom I may justly admire above all mortals beside: I may call him great, divine, or even something more; since Kepler is to be valued above the whole tribe of philosophers.
185.4: Him alone let the bards sing of.--Him alone let the philosophers read; being satisfied of this, that he who has Kepler has all things.” I quote this passage, not from the justness of the encomium it contains; for it is extravagant, and by no means true; but that the reader may see what an exalted opinion some of the greatest of the moderns have had of the genius of Kepler. “Et primum quidem de anima totius universi etsi non repugno, nihil tamen hoc libro IV. dicam.
185.5: Videtur (si est talis aliqua) in centro mundi, quod mihi sol est, residere, indeque in omnem ejus amplitudinem commercio radiorum lucis, qui sint loco spirituum in corpore animali propagari.” “Denique terræ globus tale corpus erit, quale est alicujus animalis: quodque animali est sua anima, hoc erit telluri hæc, quam quærimus, natura sublunaris.” “Videbam pleraque omnia, quæ ex corpore animantis provenientia, testantur animam in illo inesse, provenire etiam ex telluris corpore.
185.6: Ut enim corpus in cutis superficie pilos, sic terra plantas arboresque profert; inque iis ibi pediculi, hic crucæ, cicadæ, variaque insecta et monstra marina nascuntur: et ut corpus lachrymas, blennam, auriumque recrementa, est ubi et gummi ex faciei pustulis, sic tellus electrum, bitumen: utque vesica urinam, sic montes flumina fundunt; et ut corpus excrementum sulphurei odoris, crepitusque, qui etiam inflammari possunt, sic terra sulphur, ignes subterraneos, tonitrua, fulgura: utque in venis animantis generatur sanguis, et eum eo sudor, extra corpus ejectus; sic in venis terræ, metalla et fossilia, vaporque pluvius.” “Relucet igitur in anima telluris imago quædam circuli sodiaci sensibilis, totinsque adeo firmamenti, vinculum sympathiæ rerum cœlestium et terrestrium.” Proclus begins the sixth book of the following work with observing that he has celebrated in the preceding book the hebdomadic *æon* of the intellectual Gods.
185.7: The *æones* therefore, though the cause of them exists in the intelligible, properly belong to the intellectual order; and the Demiurgus or artificer of the universe subsists at the extremity of that order.
185.8: But the demiurgus according to Orpheus, prior to the fabrication of the world absorbed in himself Phanes the exemplar of the universe.
185.9: Hence he became full of ideas of which the forms in the sensible universe are the images.
185.10: And as all intellectual natures are in each, it is evident that *things which are seen were generated from the invisible æones*, conformably to the assertion of Paul.
185.11: I refer the reader who is desirous of being fully convinced of this to the notes accompanying my translation of that dialogue, in vol. 3 of my Plato.
185.13: Here we see the *æones* are acknowledged by Irenæus to be beings of an order superior to angels.
185.15: See my Collection of these Oracles in the old Monthly Magazine.
185.16: The Synoches form the second triad of the intelligible, and at the same time intellectual order of Gods.
